utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I conveyed the excuses of Mrs. Pilipovic yesterday to the Registrar. She was not sure whether she would be able to attend or not, and she conveys her excuses and wishes everyone all the best for the Easter holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stamp, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mehmed Travljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Travljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Would you -- may I invite you to make that declaration of which the text has just been handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Travljanin, the order is that you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, then by counsel for the Defence, and if it is Bench has any questions to you, we'll put them to you either at the end or during your examination. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Travljanin, would you please state your full name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Mehmed Travljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you live in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: For 50 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you employed? Do you have a job?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I am a private entrepreneur together with a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you live in Sarajevo during the period 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in that period, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have any type of role or occupation during that period?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I did after the war. But during the war, I'm afraid I don't quite understand. It's not quite clear to me what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you participate in any activity with respect to the war in Sarajevo during that period, 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, one could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In what way did you so participate?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, in the way of a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what did your functions involve being a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: My functions involved the following: To assist overcoming differences or disputes between people and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in 1994, did you have any other sort of occupation or business?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It was something like a -- it's difficult to translate. A coffee bar. Shall we call it a cafe, where we would get together? We could have some coffee or tea, talk, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, where exactly did you have this coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Very close to the place where this disaster happened. Right next to the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which disaster are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: This shell that fell there. Twenty-five metres away from where the shell fell, that is where this coffee bar I'm talking about was and where we would get together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you to describe exactly where the shop was. You have told us a distance, but could you tell us exactly where the shop was in respect to the street or the market.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, looking directly from the tram lines, my shop --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those tram lines you speak of are the tram lines on Marsala Tita Street, at the front of the market?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. If you're looking directly from those tram lines, at the front of the market. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: To make it a bit clearer, it's best to explain it starting from the tram lines. So facing from the tram lines, you see the marketplace. And to the left is this shop. And across the way on the right-hand side, about 25 metres away, is where the shell fell. And all of this is on the market itself. So shall we say it covers an area of some 400 or 500 square metres. Something like that. Don't hold me to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's get back to precisely what I was asking you about. Where exactly in relation to the market is your shop?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: On the market itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: On the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the left-hand side of the market, facing the market --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: When you're facing the market, from the tram lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is the date of the event you refer to as the disaster, is it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall the weather that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: The time was just fine for that season. There was no snow. It wasn't particularly cold either. If everything had been like the weather, it would have been fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Court what happened that day and what you experienced. Could you start with at about what time did this event occur.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, let me see. This happened about half past twelve, between half past twelve and 1.00 in the afternoon. I was sitting in my shop with some friends of mine, and like any other day, we were having the same kind of conversations, and we heard this explosion. And it was normal for us in Sarajevo in those days to hear explosions, and we would try and assess even how powerful it was. Even old women knew the type of shell, whether it was 62 or 155. This time it was a powerful one. The explosion was very powerful. We all jumped up. I looked through the window. I saw people lying down. I didn't find it unusual, because in those cases, we all throw ourselves on the ground. However, I saw no one getting up, or at least a lot of people did not get up, and then I realised what it was. We went out. It's unbelievable how quickly people arrived on the spot, reporters, cameramen. And then it was terrible, terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just tell me -- tell the Court, please, what you saw in the market. What happened when you went out?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it. I can't find the words. You have to see it. But parts of bodies were scattered around. Crying, howling, running around. People were dragging and loading. People were vomiting. What can you expect? I don't know what to say. The worst thing that could have happened, happened. It's difficult for a human mind to accept that such a thing could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said, "People were dragging and loading." What were the people dragging and loading?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The dead, the wounded. There were few wounded. I don't know exactly percentage-wise but there were quite a number of dead. They said there were 67. To me it seemed to be more, but they established that there were 67 dead. They were loading the dead onto trucks. There weren't that many vehicles. We were short of fuel. But in such cases, one finds it. Bodies were thrown one on top of another like logs, and they drove them to hospital and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, before this explosion occurred, about how many people were in the market? Could you estimate?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It's a rather difficult question. If 67 were killed, let's say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop there, please. From your observation, if any, before the explosion, are you able to make an estimation as to the amount of people who were in the market?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, there were probably 400. I couldn't tell you exactly, but it was very crowded. Let's say there were 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Not necessarily. That need not be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were the -- or what was the character of the crowd there? Was it civilian or military, or male or female? Was there any predominant group among that crowd?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Civilians, and mostly women normally because it's a market, though there were men, too, of course. But it was the centre of town. People were swapping goods, buying, selling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you notice any military activity in the vicinity of the market that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were reporters and cameramen arriving on the scene. Did they -- were there video cameramen there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did the video cameramen record the dragging and loading of the wounded and the dead?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you saw a video of what occurred, of what you saw occurred that -- would you be able to identify it and speak about it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I would ask that the video designated P2278 be shown. It's a very short video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Travljanin, is the video you saw, insofar as it concerns the market, a fair and accurate depiction of the removal of the dead and wounded that you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Just one comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wait. Before you comment --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: And to the gentleman who is interpreting there, could he speak up a little bit, please. Yes, it is all clear to me, clear as daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the market after the shell exploded?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to say. For about 45 minutes, perhaps one hour, because I had some responsibilities, too. I did not call my wife and my children immediately. And they knew that I was in the market, so I had to call them and let them know that I was safe and sound. But, say, 45 minutes to one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What about your shop? Was it damaged or not? Did anything happen to it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, it was not damaged. But one fragment nevertheless did get through the glass and landed in the wall. It wasn't fatal, however. And that is all. And I can tell you why it was so if you want to know, why the shop was not destroyed. If you want to know why, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know how much do you know, how you are familiar with that shell, how it bursts when it falls and how then the spray goes. But I was lucky with all that disaster because shells which then spray their fragments all around, they should have -- they should have also reached my shop and killed me and my friends. But it was those unfortunate -- those retched people out there who saved me, because although -- all the fragments that were flying towards my shop were absorbed by people, by people who were alive then, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall any other shelling in the vicinity of the market at about that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: You mean that same day? At that same time? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That day.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No. That day, I'm not aware of it. Even if there was something, I wouldn't be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this the first time the market had been shelled or the vicinity of the market had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall when before that the area of the market had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I do, yes. Oh, yes, I remember it very well. Before this one hit, the most fatal of all, which I think was one too many for the European Community -- but a similar shell hit the 22nd of December - that is what the shop is called - right next to the market, to the -- on the right-hand side. So my shop is on the left-hand side, and this outlet was on the right-hand side, and the market is between us. And there I will again say that as luck would have it - if that is luck - the shell did not hit the market directly. It hit the edge of the roof. And that is what saved many lives. There were dead. There were wounded. I wasn't there. I don't know how many because I wasn't on the spot. I arrived later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That shell you said which hit the 22nd of December building, about how long before the 5th of February had it fallen? Can you give us an estimated time period?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Oh, dear. Let me see. It's not -- it's difficult. I don't know because things were happening all the time right there in the centre. I don't know. I don't want to be wrong. Maybe I'll say perhaps 20 days, but don't really hold me to it, the exact date. But let us state it was some 20 days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall the -- doing a video presentation where you pointed out certain spots in the market for an OTP investigator in the latter part of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you yourself would be on that videotape?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you saw that tape, would you be able to identify yourself and the presentation you made?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I ask that videotape P3281A be shown for the Court and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The video may be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Could you please point to the location where, to the best of your recollection, you were located at the time of the explosion of the mortar at Markale Market on the 5th of February, 1994. Could you please point." "This is the place where I was." "Could you now please walk to the location where you recall seeing the mortar explode and where you saw -- later saw the crater from the mortar on the 5th of February, 1994. And when you get to that location, can you please stand on the spot."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see yourself on that videotape?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you pointed out the various places to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So at that time, at the time of the videotape, the area of the market had been rebuilt and renovated, had it not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, Mr. President. That is the end of the examination-in-chief. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. President, but may I first ask, when shall we have the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm inclined to say after your cross-examination, taking into consideration that cross-examination takes usually the same time as the examination-in-chief, but I'd say at 10.30 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I fully agree with you that we have the break immediately after my intervention, but I asked you this because this morning I wasn't able to copy all that I wanted to, and, therefore, I will perhaps, if such a need arises, I will need to ask for a break in order to copy it so as to be able to conduct my cross-examination, of course if the Chamber allows me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you need many copies, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It is a form. I simply think that I do not have enough, the sufficient number of copies. We usually have nine or ten, and I usually [as interpreted] have less. So of course it is a matter of courtesy that we have copies for everybody here. The photocopies that we -- the copies that we have here could not fit into the format of the paper that we have here, so it is a technical problem, but we shall see how we go about it. May I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning, and thank you for coming to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a certain number of questions to ask of you. You said, Witness, that you took part as a policeman in belligerencies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you were a member of the army, were you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You were merely a member of the police force, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, where was the place where -- where was your centre? Where did you gather?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: You mean as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: In the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you were not out in the country, but I'd like to say -- to know where in the city was the police barracks where you were.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It's not a barracks. It's a structure, a skyscraper. It was the centre of a neighbourhood community there, and we took over those offices. And if I told you where, I don't know that you know it. But say it was at Drvarksa Street, if you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can we know also the number of the house on the street?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know the number, but it is right there, that skyscraper, on Drvarksa Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us is it the Sarajevo centre, is it Novo Sarajevo, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Specifically to this answer [as interpreted] that you ask me, it is not easy to answer, because in Sarajevo, streets are divided into left-hand side and right-hand side, or, rather, the old town and centre. So say this was part of the old town, Stari Grad, and it was in Stari Grad and it was -- it is about, say, 300 to 400 metres away from the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, how many -- how strong was this police post? How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Do I have to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if you are telling the -- if you are speaking the truth, then you must answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please answer the questions. If you think you could not, please tell the Court, but as a rule, you should answer to all the questions. And there might be some misunderstanding. I think Mr. Piletta-Zanin is now questioning you not specifically yet on what happened at the Markale market but your activity as a policeman. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We were about 60, 65, 66 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, were these uniformed policemen?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, because we had none. Well -- so we wore whatever we had. There simply were not any uniforms around. Had there been any uniforms, we would have been uniformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you telling us that none of the 60 or 70 policemen who were based in the street that you mention, that none of them wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, there were none, as I said. And we are not policemen. We are a group of enthusiasts defending at that time. At that time, we didn't know what the police was. We didn't know what the police job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But, Witness, tell us then, what were you if you were not a policeman? I understood that you were a policeman. Was it a special unit?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know how to tell you. A special policeman. After all, we were all policemen, but we were the official ones, unlike other policemen. You didn't understand my point. I wasn't a professional. I became one only when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You tell me that there were, therefore, official policemen and unofficial policemen, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Naturally. Naturally. Those who were policemen before the war, then they went on as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you are telling me that you were not, or at least that is what emerges, what was passed from the transcript, that you were not a policeman. At the time of the incident, that is 5th of -- 5th of February, 1994, you were not a policeman. What were you? You weren't?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Until when were you a policeman, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Until the end of 1993. I believe it was October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And when you say a "policeman," Witness, what do you exactly mean by that word "policeman"?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, if you talk about the rule of law in a state, then I can tell you that under such circumstances -- I don't know. What exactly do you want to know? Are we talking about wartime, what a "policeman" means in wartime? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you tell me, in wartime, was a policeman a soldier? Is that how I'm to take your hesitance?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. I mean, a policeman is somebody who is at hand, who helps, who comes to succour, who does things like that. As for the site itself, it was not defence line, it was the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, but until 1993, were you insured? Were you a beneficiary of social insurance?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: None of us were, not only me. It was later on, and it varied then on the companies as they started to pay in. And there's still very many people who are still not insured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. But formally speaking, were you -- did you -- did you hold the thing which is usually called the social card, the social insurance card?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Nobody held it. I repeat, nobody held those. And had something happened, there was no problem. You'd go to the hospital, and they'd do whatever was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And if you went to hospital, nobody would ask who was paying your insurance for you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Oh, come. No. No. It was wartime, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And is it that there were never some forms, Witness, which would indicate the existence of such-and-such insurance -- insurer?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't think so. Perhaps, but I can't really say because it was a time of confusion. There was no red tape or anything. I mean, it was a time when people's lives were being saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, your activities until 1993 -- until the end of 1993, you said that you were a kind of parallel police, if I understand you properly. Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Let me correct you. We were not parallel police. There was just one police. And I was armed. I had a short barrel. But I was lucky enough that I did have it. Very many of my fellow policemen didn't have them. We simply tried to arm ourselves in all ways possible, but it was with great difficulty that we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since you had no uniforms and since you were not a parallel police, as you say, then how did people identify you as a policeman, not parallel but armed policeman? How did -- how could people tell you apart?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: We had our accreditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And by "accreditation," I presume you mean a card that you could wear, for instance, on your chest. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. With a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I see. With your photograph.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us something about the structure that was called the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, say that -- that we did -- were a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. But it changed. Initially, it was the Territorial Defence. And then things became a little clearer, because we changed our accreditation several times. As the things improved, we changed it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer. You are telling us, Witness, that you were armed, that you had a weapon. Do you know if the Territorial Defence was in the possession of its own weapons, for its own purpose? That is, did the Territorial Defence have its own arsenal?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "no," does that mean that you do not know that or does it mean that they did not have them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... have it. No, we know that they didn't have much, because everything had been taken away from us in the city of Sarajevo, and we tried to manage. I presume that some people had their personal weapons before the war, and they used them. But the city, the state --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Yes. I am interrupting you because I see on the -- on the transcript that your answer is not recorded in full. Will you please start your answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment: The answers are not fully recorded because the counsel starts speaking before the witness has finished his answer.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: There were no weapons. There were no arsenals, and not enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the interpreters indicate that one of the reasons that they are not able to translate is that because you start asking the next question before the answer of the witness has been translated. So would you please make a pause between the answer and your next question. And perhaps may I ask this to you, as well, Mr. Travljanin. Everything has to be translated. So once the question has been put to you, perhaps you could look at your screen. Do you have a text moving in front of you? If you'd wait --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I do not understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if you just wait until it stops moving, that means that everything has been translated up to that moment. And if you're done, give your answers. And you'll certainly forget about it sooner or later. Then I'll remind you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And my apologies for it. It is quite true that perhaps I was too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You were telling us that the Territorial Defence was not armed. Do you know if in the structure of the former Yugoslavia it was true that the Defence, generally speaking, was organised on the three tiers, on three -- was based on three pillars: The army, which at times is called JNA; the Territorial Defence, which was the second pillar; and the civil defence, which was the third pillar of the defence? Would that defence philosophy more or less reflect what you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: You are correct in saying that in the former state in Yugoslavia, that it existed. There was the Yugoslav army, the Territorial Defence, and the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your answer. And in relation to what is called -- or rather, what you call the TO, that is, the Territorial Defence, do you know if at the time it was true that the weapons were kept in some large public companies so that they could be used if need arose, so that they could be used if need arose, in case of some trouble? Does that remind you of something?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In work organisations, yes, that is true of them. But they had been removed in the time by the other side. They had taken away everything -- they had seized and taken away everything from us. I could take a whole day telling you about all this, but this suffices. We did not have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, which is quite complete. I know who you mean when you said "the other side." I assume you meant the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the Serb side. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, as a participant in the Territorial Defence, did you know whether the Territorial Defence was able to be used to support the army in case of war, in case of combat?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It's very difficult to answer that question. There was a quest for weapons. We were looking for weapons. We couldn't do anything without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when I ask you this question, I'm not talking simply about armed support, but one could also provide logistic support. For example, provide means of communication, various rear support methods. So do you know whether the Territorial Defence in the broad sense supported the army in operations of a military kind?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: That's a very delicate question for me to answer, because I'm not qualified to do so. But if you're asking my personal opinion as a citizen --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But let's take your personal example, Witness. There were at least 60 or 70 people that you knew and who were located some 300 metres from the Markale marketplace and who were part of the Territorial Defence. Did you know other people who were also members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Of course I did. There were many headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Fine. So when you're talking about many headquarters or locations where the Territorial Defence was situated, could you indicate them to us, please, Witness, since apparently you were aware of them and you knew them.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: We're delving deep into the Territorial Defence. I think we're going in the wrong direction, because every skyscraper, every house, had its own guards who took turns. There was so much fear that people were guarding buildings overnight. You can't call that Territorial Defence. They were patriots. There was no difference any more amongst us. We all were -- wanted to save our town and to save ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, these patriots, as you call them and who were guards, they were therefore armed, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Of course they were. There were representatives of all three nations. There were Serbs, too, because people were afraid for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if we're talking here about patriots who were not members of the Territorial Defence or of the police or soldiers, were they then armed civilians? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: There were some weapons here and there, just for the psychological effect it would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: These armed civilians you're talking about, could you distinguish them by a distinctive sign, a label, something that they wore on their chest?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you yourself - and you are telling us that you were not a policeman but a member of the Territorial Defence - did you consider yourself to be a civilian or a military man?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. You're talking about the Territorial Defence and the policemen. I told you I was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, in your capacity as a member of the Territorial Defence that you were --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: At the beginning, this didn't last long. Afterwards, I became a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Fine. At the beginning. At the beginning. In your capacity as a member of the Territorial Defence, did you consider yourself to be a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: We all thought we were soldiers for the defence. I see that that is what you are alluding to. Yes, a soldier. I considered myself a soldier. I was proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I understand you now. You consider yourself to be a soldier, though you were not formally incorporated in the army.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: You were talking about the very beginning. There were no military formations. I am also talking about the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am talking about the beginning. So regarding the beginning, we agree. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, this beginning, until when did it last, this initial period?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, almost for a whole year, until the army was constituted and the police force, which I was a member. And then things started functioning, though there were omissions, shortages of weapons and food and everything. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You say for about a year, as I see in the transcript. Can we agree, then, that the war unfortunately started in your region in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, if you were to give a date for the beginning of the conflict in Sarajevo, to the best of your recollection, what would it be?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Let's say officially the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, before the 4th of April, 1992, a little before that, was there a highly conflictual situation which was almost like a war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. You're right. There was panic. It could be felt in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you in two words indicate those few days or few weeks before the date that you have mentioned, the 4th of April, what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I'll be brief and concrete, to the point as to what was happening. The Serbs -- can I use that word? The Serbs took up some checkpoints on the other side of Vrbanja. They had socks on their heads. We thought that they were playing around. They started banning passage, movement. Nobody really knew what was really happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we're still talking about this period from the spring of 1992 until the spring of 1993. Do you know whether in Sarajevo, in addition to the armed civilians that we referred to a moment ago, were there any militia of a paramilitary kind?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: If we're talking about the very beginning, there were quite a number of groups. You may misunderstand me, you may take me wrong, but all those groups were working in the interest of the defence of the town and the people of Sarajevo, regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware of irregulars that were fully armed and that were situated in Sarajevo? Are you aware of such groups? When I say "irregulars," I means groups that were not integrated within the Territorial Defence or later within the army or the Civil Defence.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about the very beginnings. At the very beginning there was nothing. All this was in embryonic form. So if a group is next to me, I can't say that it is a parallel group or something like that. I am saying, from the beginning, we all rose up in defence. And later on we knew who was a policeman, who was a member of the army, who belonged to the Civil Defence, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, so from your answer, I gather that you never heard mention, while you were a member of the Territorial Defence, groups that were irregulars and which were waging their own war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I am repeating again. If we're talking about the very beginning, there were such groups but not irregular groups. And they were not waging their own wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware of a commander called Juka?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. But many don't know who Juka was. I don't know whether Their Honours know who Juka was. May I tell them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Juka, many people think he was a bandit, a thief. Before the war, he did all kinds of things and that's quite true. But -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: That same Juka, when the first shot was fired and when serious things started happening, with his so-called thieves and paramilitary, as you call them, units stood up in defence of the city and he saved Sarajevo from the first onslaught, and that is a fact. He is deceased. He has died. And we have to stop there, and we have to pay tribute to him for this. As for other things that he did, he deserves punishment. That is who Juka was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why should we stop there? You consider Juka to be a hero?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: For a period of time, he was a hero indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know other chiefs coming from the same origins as this Juka that we have mentioned: Caco, Delte, Labudovic, Seve, Nedo, Akrapi?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. I've heard of them, of course. Every citizen of Sarajevo knows about them, Juka and Caco and Celo. I repeat again - I'm going back to the very beginning - those men defended indeed the town. I never saw a pistol. I did serve the army in Tito's days. I wasn't interested in weapons. I didn't even know how to shoot. But these men were brave. And with the former army in the very centre of town, they were the ones who gave us hope and will, and we followed them. As to what happened later, it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer, but I gather from that answer that these commanders whose names I have listed and who you say you knew, headed armed groups.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, correct. At the very beginning. We're still talking about the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were those people heavily armed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No. I don't know what you mean by "heavily."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were organised amongst themselves in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, let's say so. Juka had quite a good group around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "a good group," how many people would you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: At first, probably about 200 men who joined them. And there was some discipline. He took people from the former army who had some knowledge and capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you're talking about a group in the order of 200 men, they were under this single commander?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about Juka. He may have had more than that. Maybe more. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, so you're telling us there may be more. Could you give us some indication of the size?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I repeat, they were not irregular units. At first we were all regulars, indeed regulars. Regulars indeed. I didn't have a chance, an opportunity to join Juka. I was over here on the other side. I would have though. Maybe I would have left him later on, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, concerning the other groups that we mentioned a moment ago who were under these other commanders that I mentioned, were they of the same size roughly? I'm talking about the troops under them.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, I think there was a difference, after all, between them. After all, Juka was the leading person. These others were below him. So there was a kind of difference amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you believe that Juka had authority over all the other groups?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, not really, but his opinion was obeyed. And I am repeating again, at the very, very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, I should now like to go on to another line of questioning, and I am interested in the weapons in the centre of Sarajevo. Witness, do you know whether what are sometimes called defenders, which I will use exceptionally now, the defenders of Sarajevo, did they have a special unit of so-called snipers?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether there was a factory in Sarajevo called Zrak?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Before the war, yes. The former Yugoslav army held it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did this factory produce highly specialised optical sights for weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: For the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question was not whether it was working for the Yugoslav army. My question was whether it manufactured this type of product. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: You mean during the war? I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You don't know whether the factory was producing optical sights?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: During the war, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And before the war, did it produce optical sights?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did this factory continue working until the beginning of the war, right up until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In whose hands was the factory when the two camps split up? Shall we call it that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: At the moment of the split, it was probably under the Yugoslav army. But when they separated, it was on our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "our territory," you mean the territory controlled --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I mean the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. So it was under the control of Sarajevo. Do you know in whose hands the stockpiles were?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the stockpiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I should like to go on to another area. You were in the Territorial Defence throughout this period. Could you confirm that there was no fuel that was readily available throughout the period of the war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just -- just -- I am hesitant to rise because I want my friend to proceed as quickly as possible, but I think the question could be a little bit clearer. It's a little vague when he asks him about being in the Territorial Defence throughout this period. If perhaps we could narrow the period to know what he's asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President, but I think on the French channel it was much clearer. So I can ask the Prosecution to follow the French channel, because he will be able to follow much better what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you suggesting that someone -- Mr. Stamp, I never noticed that you speak or understand French. Is that true or is that not true?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not good enough for these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't ask someone to listen in a language he doesn't master. Of course, if there's a difference you may point at that, but you can't require someone to speak or understand a language he --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought that Mr. Stamp's French was good enough for him to be able to follow. So I apologise to Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I never heard Mr. Stamp speaking or listening to French so that I assumed that he was not able to do so. But perhaps I underestimated him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One should never underestimate the Prosecution. And I'm very sorry, Mr. Stamp. If I may, I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, during the period we're interested in - and that is the beginning of the war until the autumn of 1994 - were you still in Sarajevo? I thought you said you were.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Since during this period you were in Sarajevo, when was there a shortage of petrol? Could you confirm that it was not readily available?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It was hard. It was hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness. Do you have any knowledge of the existence of mortars in the possession of the military authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: At the beginning, no. But later, yes. I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Do you know or did you see -- but first, do you know whether certain people had light mortars which they could move around in vehicles of the Golf brand, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, no. That's very risky.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "no," does that mean that you don't know, or you're telling us that that was never the case?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Witness. I should now like to show you, Witness, a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is an exhibit that has already been produced, and the number is D70. But as this witness may be led to make certain markings, I am reproducing the document without the number so that it shouldn't be confused with the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not quite sure any more whether there was already any marking made on that map. I -- my recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's on the map, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has not been marked by anyone, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite correct. I don't know whether we can use it again such as it is. Could we check that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There have been no markings made on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then of course we now use a new copy of that same -- well, it's not a -- of that same document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what will then be the new number?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem, because I saw in the transcript "D80" but I think that we have reached D79. I'm not quite sure about the numbering by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even if a document is not admitted, it keeps its number. Therefore, D79 was not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So it will be D81, therefore. I haven't premarked it because I wasn't sure. But I can do that right now, Mr. President. In the meantime, I would like to request the usher to be kind enough to come to the Defence Bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so that I can give him the documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the witness is hearing me.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have in front of you a document consisting of two diagrams: The first document, consisting of two pages; and the -- it should be read together -- and a second diagram, which is the last page of this document. So Witness, could you look at the third page, please, the one at the end of the document. Would you tell us what you see there, please, whether you recognise this drawing.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And if you do, then please tell us what it could be.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Probably the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's a Markale, is it not, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His excellency General Galic would like to ask this document to be placed on the ELMO, please, so that everyone can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please just point. And you will be also given a black marker. Will you please show us where was your coffee-shop on this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could turn it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, do that. Do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Because I think that would be easier for everybody. Like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just wait. Just wait, Witness. Let me finish my question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have another five minutes -- five, perhaps eight minutes at the outside. So this is the time for the break, and I do not know whether it is better to take the break now, which is an important thing, and that we then come back to this when we return or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it will be better to have a break now. Mr. Travljanin, we'll have a break for half an hour. So you return then, and then the examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin will continue. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, before I give you the opportunity to resume your cross-examination and before the witness comes into the courtroom, I'd like to come back to the objection of Mr. Stamp in respect of your question. Let me just try to find it. Your question would read in the English transcript -- the transcript reads, page 29, line 9: "You were in the Territorial Defence throughout this period. Could you confirm that there was no fuel that was readily available throughout the period of the war in Sarajevo?" Mr. Stamp objected on the basis that the question could be clearer. Mr. Stamp says: "It's a little vague when he asks him about being in the Territorial Defence throughout this period," and he asked for narrowing the question. I think Mr. Stamp had in mind at that moment that the witness has said a couple of times that he was only during a certain period in the Territorial Defence and not during the whole period of the war. You responded, and let me -- by saying: "I'm sorry, Mr. President, but I think on the French channel it was much clearer. So I can ask the Prosecution to follow the French channel because he'll be able to follow much better what I'm saying." But, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, didn't you say, and say it in French: "[Interpretation] You were in the Territorial Defence throughout this period of time. Can you confirm it for me that there was no petrol readily available in Sarajevo throughout the war?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already said that I have full confidence in this Chamber, so no doubt if you say that I said that, then undoubtedly I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you said, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. That means that the French text was in no way clearer than the English transcript. So it was improper to tell Mr. Stamp that he could better listen to the French channel, and it was especially improper because there's an underlying suggestion that the translation would not have been made according to the standards which we expect in this courtroom. That's the reason why you should not have referred Mr. Stamp to the French channel, indirectly blaming the translators for giving a not precise translation. Could the witness be brought in the courtroom again. And you may proceed with your cross-examination, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I repeat what I said, that is, I address my apologies to everybody concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please be seated, Mr. Travljanin. It was a bit more than half an hour, but we had to deal with a technical question meanwhile. So we apologise for that. Please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we shall resume. I believe you have on the screen -- I believe we can still see it. I don't know, however. Yes, we do. We see a sketch here. Will you merely show us where was your coffee-shop? Of course if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: And shall I put a black cross there or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. Wait. Wait. Wait, please. Please check that it is the right colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I then ask the usher to check, because I cannot see from here whether the colour of the marker is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a problem, since my laptop was not connected. But I fixed it. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't dare suggest that you move -- change to the French channel, but I -- Mr. President, I was saying that we should check the colour of the marker. [In English] Is it a black one or -- is it black? Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: A black marker, a black one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you then use this marker, please, to mark the place where the coffee-shop was which you ran.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do it, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: If we assume and we know that these are the -- these are the tram lines, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But I suppose you know the area better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. So these are the tram tracks. And we are entering the market from the tram lines, moving into the interior, to the left. So these are stalls here. And this part here -- now, I don't know how you drew this. It should be narrower than it is here. But it doesn't matter. And the outlet ought to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for being so precise. I'd like you now to look at what you call the stalls, that is, these rectangular boxes which are in the market. Please look at them.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would this distribution of stalls tell you the distribution of stalls on the day of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. Will you please, then, put your signature at the bottom of the document. Will you please sign this document -- of course, if the Chamber gives -- if Their Honours give their leave for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't mind. We never do it. But I don't see any specific reason, since the exhibit has a number. So that's the only marking on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So it is not worth the trouble. There's no need to sign it. Will you then -- will you then, please, go back to the previous page, or more exactly, the page which we see here. Witness, do you see here in this part of the sketch to the right the building of the 22nd of December, which is partially sketched, and the other building where your coffee-shop was on the other side? Thank you. Witness, the distribution of this stall which are represented by these rectangular boxes, does this tally with your memory?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No. I think that more stalls have been crowded into here. But it could be -- no. I mean, when one looks at it with the lay eye, one could see that there are just too many stalls, but more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions with regard to this document, Mr. President. We don't have -- it can be removed from the ELMO. If the usher would be so kind to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, the coffee-shop that you ran, for how long did you run it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, when I got off this police service that I did, and that was 1993. October, maybe September -- October. I'm not sure about the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know who ran this coffee-shop before you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Nobody. It was completely destroyed. It was completely gutted out. It used to be a fishmonger's. And then with the help of my friends, I restored it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But the owner, who was the owner?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No. The owner is not known to this day. We're still waiting for the restitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could it be that the -- its owner was somebody of Serb origin?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Oh, dear. Yes. Yes, it could be. I can't say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, before we put on the ELMO another document, which is a map of Sarajevo, I'd like you to answer the following question: Do you know why and when the commander whom I mentioned a moment ago, Caco, and whom you said that you knew, do you know when he was removed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I did not hear the witness say that he knew this commander. I think he said he heard of him and knew of him. There's a slight distinction between knowing somebody and knowing of the person or hearing of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah. Well, I do not really know what is the term that I used in French. But I can rephrase this question. I shall be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The person that we're talking about, Witness, that person whose name you just heard and you told us that you knew it - and I mean the name - and you said Caco something, that he was your commander, that he was --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if this commander was removed from his post at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know when that happened, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know which year?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Even there I'd be wrong. But I'd say it was towards the very end, that is, sometime -- at about the time of the Dayton Accords. I don't know exactly, but I think it was towards the very end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And if I give you the date, which is October 1993, would you say that that was it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think that is the correct date. I think he lived after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And do you know why he was removed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: You're asking me why he was dismissed. I was just an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Another question: Are you aware of a shelling which happened -- which hit a green area in Grbavica some -- that when some 30 shells were launched by Sarajevo forces?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't come as a surprise. You could find as many places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But if I mention the date of the 24th of May, would that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know where the headquarters of the 9th Motorised Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will now have a map shown you, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that we have enough copies for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you numbered the document, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D82. Thank you, registrar, as always.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this map which is now on the video monitor?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Will you then use a pointer which the usher will place in your hand in order to point at where do you situate Markale on this map?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't see Stari Grad, the old town, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Perhaps -- [In English] On that -- on the very centre of the map.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it is a good idea to zoom it in. As you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Stop. Stop, stop. [Interpretation] And now we have to move the map higher up.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it has to be moved up because this is Skenderija. We have to cross Miljacka. Let me see. Brajkovic, no. Cicin Han, no. And further on, the map has to be moved down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is the usher who has to do it or the technical booth. [In English] The upper part. The upper part of the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It has to be moved down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: A little bit. A little bit. And a little bit, and here we are. Stop.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Here we are. Yes. We're quite near. This is Mejtas, Bascarsija. And there's the street where yet another tragedy, a horrible tragedy, happened in Ferhadija. I'm sure everybody here is aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, will you please -- do you see a street in?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Mula Mustafe Baseskije. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And will you please now find the site of Markale?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I can't really -- I'm reading this. I think this is it, where it says "104." It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On that street that you just-- that you've just mentioned, will you please -- do you see a sign indicating a church? Can you see it? This is a black symbol, a black rectangle with a white cross, and it is right below two letters, "MU." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: No, I don't. I just don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you see the street which we're talking about which was the former Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And will you take your pointer and point on the screen. Not on the screen, on the other screen. Will you please indicate the street? Yes. Stop. Stop now and keep the pointer there. Here to the left you have a church. Do you see it? There. Thank you. And in relation to the church, can you locate the location of Markale?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: If we look at it like this, the church should be to the right. It is so-called cathedral. So the market is to the left of the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: A bit to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Will you then please put a cross at the place where you believe that the Markale market was on this map?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure I really hit it. I'll -- right. I'm afraid I'll go wrong. I know the street and that is where it should be, approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Please put a cross. Will you please make a cross on there? Or if you would rather put a circle, I will accept that, too. You can put a circle there --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Here it was, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: -- for the transcript. Yes. We are aware where that is. Thank you. Witness, will you please show where the street where the headquarters of the Territorial Defence was, the one that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Sir, I think you just went off the mark. I repeat that we didn't have headquarters, because I was part of the police. The Territorial Defence lasted for a very short time, and it changed from one place to the other. It moved house frequently. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, but witness, I will interrupt you. No. Excuse me. A moment ago, told us about a place where there were about 60, 65 persons. Will you please point at the -- at this place, repeat the name of the street, please?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can point at it, but you keep asking me about --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which is the street please?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It is the former Drvarska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Former Drvarksa Street. Thank you. Will you please point at that street? Please take the pointer and point at that street on the map which is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I can't really get my bearings here. If that -- if this is the market, then we go up. I don't see it say "Drvarksa Street." Is it the new plan or the -- the new map or the old map?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: This is a new map, I believe, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. These are the new names of the streets. They have changed those names. So it is above the market. I mean, there can be no mistake about that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
