utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us whether in relation to the market that road was to the north, to the south, to the east, or to the west of the market in relation to the Markale marketplace?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you, because I may make a mistake, but to the left in relation to the market. Perhaps a little to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you said a moment ago it was about 300, 400 metres away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. From the scene of the event.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. My last question: When the accident occurred in Markale, did you know whether there was a factory for the army situated in the building of the 22nd of December?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It is still there, the building, but it's not a factory. Former. It was a former factory of the Yugoslav People's Army, which manufactured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there workers in that building and in that factory?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I can't tell you. Probably there were some guards. It wasn't empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But, Witness, your coffee-shop was opposite this building, opposite this factory, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It's not a factory. You keep saying things. It's not a factory. We can't call it a factory. A former factory, call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President. That ends my cross-examination, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no re-examination. However, may I ask two further questions which don't necessarily arise out of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Looking at the clock and knowing that it's the last witness, and taking into account you took 34 minutes for your examination-in-chief and the cross-examination took one hour and 18 minutes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Travljanin, immediately before the explosion at Markale market, did you hear anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. What -- what could I have heard? Something unusual, you mean? Unusual things were happening from one minute to the next, so I couldn't tell you specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Having been a resident of Sarajevo during the war, were you accustomed to being in places that had been hit by mortars or being near where mortar shells impacted?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: That is the right question. It's strange what people are like. One gets used to everything, even to shells. One minute you're alive, the next you're dead. The only thing that mattered is that it wasn't you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when mortar shells impact, do you sometimes hear anything at about the time when they impact?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Let me see. If you hear this so-called something else that you're referring to, some kind of sound, it's a good thing when you hear it. It means it's flown by, and once it impacts, it's too late. I know that from personal experience. Not just me, the whole town, children, old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What type of sound? And Mr. Travljanin, please listen precisely to the question I'm -- please listen to the questions I'm asking and answer precisely. You said if you hear this sound, it's a good thing. What is the sound that you sometimes hear when a mortar impacts?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It's called whistle. It's like a whistle. Children were able to imitate it, this sound of a shell. And there were jokes being cracked. Something like this, like a whistle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said that this was something that was very common for the residents of Sarajevo to hear and know and recognise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It was part of everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the -- in respect of the incident of the 5th of February, did you hear a whistle?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: I did not, no. No. I said a moment ago when you hear the whistle, it's gone. But once it hits, it's over. Some other people somewhere else heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. When the explosion occurred, you were inside your shop; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Travljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Any reason to cross-examine the witness on this particular aspect touched upon during the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I had difficulty in following the question, because there was reference to the impact. But anyway, I don't think it requires any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Travljanin, the other Judges don't have any questions for you, but I have got one question for you. You testified that when you heard the explosion, you were sitting in your shop and that you looked out of the window and that only then you went out. On the video, you were asked where you were during the explosion, and you indicated a place which seemed to me to be outside the shop. If you'd like to review it, I'll ask this part of the video to be replayed. Perhaps it's better to do it. Could we perhaps replay the video of the -- the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, I believe, is Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have known it by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the interview with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could that please be replayed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I comment on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "... the location of the mortar on Markale market on the 5th of February, 1994? Could you please point." "This is the place that I was." "Could you now please walk to the location where you recall seeing -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't need to be further played. Yes. Thank you. You're pointing with your hand to what seemed to be the back of you. Could you explain exactly what you pointed at when the investigator was in Sarajevo and in respect of what you testified in this court.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is my premises. Those are my premises. The question was where I was at the moment of the explosion, and I pointed with my hand. You saw the premises behind me. That is where I had this coffee-shop, and that is where I was. And then you see on the video that I went on to show where the shell fell. So that's it. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that when pointing with your hand to the building behind you, you mentioned to indicate that -- you meant to indicate that you were inside that building.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: It's not a building. It's a small coffee-shop, my coffee-shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in your coffee-shop. Yes. Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED TRAVLJANIN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Travljanin, you've now answered all the questions put to you by both the Prosecution and the Defence and from the Bench. I thank you very much for coming to The Hague. Judges are dependent on the information they get from those who know about what happened, and your answers to the questions give us information we need while preparing the decisions we have to take. So thank you so much for assisting the Tribunal in this way to fulfil its task. And I wish you a safe journey home and a good Easter weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3281A, videotape; Exhibit P2278, videotape; Exhibit D81, three pages of diagram of Markale Market marked by witness; D82, map marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All these documents and tapes are admitted into evidence. Mr. Stamp, I do understand that you've run out of witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Unhappily, perhaps, we have run out of witnesses. We tried to schedule to ensure that no one would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- have to wait for the long weekend here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a full understanding for that. We can't just play around with witnesses. We have to take into consideration that we can't keep them here for too long a time. Is there anything else the parties would bring to the attention of the Chamber at this very moment? You're both standing. Mr. Stamp, you're -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Because for once we have gained a bit of time, I have two remarks to make. One is that once again that we, as the Defence, in order to examine this witness, we needed to have certain elements which were not given to us. And I'm referring to the totality of the exhibits that we know that exist, and those are the military directives which we have been requesting for -- from the general headquarters right down to the brigade level. I would have liked to ask certain questions in that connection; however, the Defence's wings were cut, and we repeat that. And we should like to ask the Prosecution two things through Mr. Stamp: First, when will the Defence finally have access to these exhibits which are of absolutely vital importance for them, because we can work 24 hours a day, if necessary. And my second question: In order to prepare ourselves better, can we know how the Prosecution will act in the future regarding medical documents? Often the translations are often inventions. And I think this is a term that you used yourself. I think I'm speaking from memory. I think that is the word that you used. So can the Prosecution tell us regarding these two groups of documents what they intend to do. Can they assist the Defence regarding this particular question regarding multiple translations of exhibits; and secondly, when we will have access to documents of a military nature. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect of the first question, we have disclosed all documents which ought to be disclosed pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Anything which we receive in future - because this is on ongoing obligation - which is relevant or ought to be disclosed pursuant to those Rules will immediately be disclosed. In respect to the second question, the translation department is a department which operates under the direction of the Registry, not the Office of the Prosecutor. And I did indicate on a previous occasion when a part of a document had been translated and not all of it. In other words, only the relevant part had been translated and not the amount of stitches or the precise amount of penicillin that had been prescribed. That if there are issues in respect to translations, those issues must be brought to the CLSS so that they may take whatever action that needs to be done. I don't think it is quite fair to be making statements which might adversely characterise their performance unless they are brought here or are put in a position where they can answer these questions. In any case, I am quite sure, and I've been informed that they are well prepared to accommodate the Defence and have done so in other cases if the Defence brings any discrepancy or any issues to their attention. May it please Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. President, I'm sorry, but simply this: Regarding the so-called military documents, I note that the Prosecution has said that they will disclose them as soon as they have them. I know that there is a case called Kordic in which those documents have been disclosed. Therefore, the Prosecution does have possession of those documents, and I think they should authorise access to them. Regarding translations, we understand that we are not accusing anyone among the translators. On the other hand, the Prosecution produces certain exhibits, and that is up to them. But sometimes they contain translations that are relevant to other documents. And so if there's an error, I think it doesn't come from the translators but from the actual Prosecution, which gave one document thinking that it was another document. So the Defence, like anyone else, would like to have the clearest possible situation. It's a question of methodology, which affects in the first place the Prosecution. Of course, the Defence never said that it was criticising the work of anyone, certainly not of the translators. That is not something that we have said, and we wouldn't like those words to be put in our mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me deal with both the problems raised by Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Let me first stress that it is the task of the Defence itself to find whatever documents that could support the case of the Defence. I'd like to start saying this, because I'd like to stress that the Defence should take all efforts, and the Defence is aware of all the rules they can invoke if they have difficulties in finding what they are seeking. Of course, this Chamber will always consider requests for assistance if the Defence finds difficulties in its task. If the Defence is of the opinion, as you expressed referring to the Kordic case, that the Prosecution has in its possession documents that are material for the Defence and might even be - that's how I understand it - might even be exculpatory, then of course there is a general obligation to disclose whatever exculpatory evidence is in the hands of the Prosecution. I did understand that the Prosecution is doing its utmost best to locate whatever documents the Defence has referred to. And I think we are still waiting for the results of this first round of inspection of what is in the hands of the Prosecution, and I expect that this will be done soon. We discussed and we got an indication from the Prosecution when they thought they could have finished this exercise, so I expect on rather short notice a report both of the Prosecution in respect of the results and, if necessary, any comment from the Defence. You will understand that talking about the totality of exhibits is, well, a rather vague denotation. And of course, if, for example, specific documents in the Kordic case are referred to, I do assume that the Defence has given every detail which they have to the Prosecution in order to better enable the Prosecution to undertake what it promised to undertake. Let me then go to the second issue, the medical documents. We have been confronted a few times with differences in translation and even translated parts of a document where we could not find a corresponding text in the copy of the original of which it was translated. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have heard the decisions of this Chamber about this -- of these translations. I think it would be proper for the Defence that whenever they are confronted with this situation, that they immediately inform the Prosecutor. And if the translations are made on the request of the Prosecution, I think it's proper that the Prosecution then addresses those who are responsible for the translations made on their request. If this is done well in advance of the documents being tendered as evidence, then we can avoid a situation where we're not -- this Chamber's not only confronted with the problems in respect of translation or -- well, let me say in general the problems about the translation, but that we can proceed in such a way that the Prosecution has been able to repair, as far as possible, what has done and that there is a final translation which could be checked by the Defence on its correctness. So therefore, I think the first thing to be done is that whenever you are confronted with such a situation, immediately inform the Prosecutor, see what can be done so that we have a proper translation at the trial. This of course does not prevent you from indicating later on that this final translation is the result of earlier complaints by the Defence on the earlier translations, but then at least we can proceed and the Prosecution is able to properly prepare for that situation during the examination of the witness. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor -- sorry. Mr. President. Sorry. I was listening to the interpretation. I was listening to the interpretation, hence the error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They both start with "P-r." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We hold in high esteem both, in high regard both. Now the question. What I wanted to say is the following: that the Prosecutor, as I was just saying, was clearly informed in a general manner, and since December last year, that infinite problems arise with every medical document which is poorly legible or illegible. We are speaking in general terms. Of course the Defence could take up each one of these documents, but since we do not know what the Prosecution will be producing and not, will be tendering or not, and you could see yesterday that several documents were in extremis withdrawn by the Defence, however, it is a considerable effort on the part of the Defence to take all medical documents and to say, "This one is all right, and this one is not." We're talking in principle and in general. I think that the Prosecution, as they had done in the beginning, to find the most legible of the copies and to supply it both to the interpreters, to the Chamber, and to the Defence. And the Defence would appreciate it highly, but we will resist on this, and we thank you very much for your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have taken notice of your observations in this respect. Then if there's nothing else to be raised at this very moment, we are just before the Easter weekend. I wish everyone in this courtroom, those who assist us just outside of this courtroom, a good Easter weekend. General Galic, the same is true for you. I do understand that under your circumstances it is not the Easter weekend someone wishes to have, but I nevertheless wish you a good Easter weekend. We will resume --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My Easter will be somewhat later, but we shall mark this one too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until next Tuesday at a quarter past two in this same courtroom, if I'm correct, Madam Registrar. Yes. We will adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of April, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.03 p.m.,
